title: Bakery Bestsellers
story: You run a small bakery, and the till keeps a log with one line per item sold: croissant, scone, croissant, bagel, and so on. The front window only has room for a few trays.
Before tomorrow you want to know which items sold the most today, so they get the window. You do not care how they are ranked among themselves, only which ones make the cut.
task: Write bestsellers(sales, k). Return the k items that appear most often in sales, in any order, each item once.
The input is chosen so the answer is unique: the k-th best item always sold strictly more than the item in place k + 1.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ number of different items in sales
Item names are non-empty lowercase strings.
The set of the k most sold items is unique.

examples.explanation: Counts: croissant 3, scone 2, bagel 1, muffin 1. The two bestsellers are croissant and scone. Returning ["scone", "croissant"] is just as correct.
Donut sold 3, bagel 2, eclair 1. Bagel was sold first, but donut sold the most.

hints: Before you can pick the top items, what number do you need to know for every item? How would you get it in one pass over the log?
Count with a map from item to count. Now the problem is: given those counts, pick the k biggest. Sorting the items by count works. Can you avoid a full sort?
No count can be bigger than sales.length. What if you made one bucket for every possible count, and dropped each item into the bucket for its count?

Build the count map. Then make a list of buckets indexed 0 to sales.length, where bucket c holds the items sold exactly c times. Walk the buckets from the highest count down, collecting items until you have k.
bruteForce: Take each different item, count it by scanning the whole log, and then repeatedly pick the item with the largest count that you have not picked yet.

Counting each item by rescanning costs O(n) per item, so O(n · m) for m different items. With 100,000 sales and thousands of items that is hundreds of millions of steps. Counting once with a map, then sorting the m items by count, gets you to O(n + m log m), which is fine. Buckets remove even the sort.

walkthrough: There are two steps: count every item, then pick the biggest counts. Counting is one pass with a map. For picking, notice that counts are small whole numbers between 1 and n, so you can file items by count instead of sorting them.
Trace [scone, croissant, bagel, croissant, scone, croissant, muffin] with k = 2:
• Buckets (0 to 7): bucket 1 = [bagel, muffin], bucket 2 = [scone], bucket 3 = [croissant], the rest empty.
• Walk down from bucket 7. Buckets 7 to 4 are empty. Bucket 3 gives croissant.
• Bucket 2 gives scone. Now there are 2 items, so stop: [croissant, scone].

Sorting the m different items by count is a perfectly good answer too, and in an interview it is often what people write first. A heap of size k is the other common choice when k is much smaller than m.
solution.timeWhy: One pass to count, one pass over at most n buckets, and each item is placed once.
solution.spaceWhy: The count map and the n + 1 buckets.
solution.takeaway: For "most frequent" questions, count with a hash map first, then select. When the values you rank by are small integers (like counts up to n), bucketing by value replaces sorting.
